newsitem.title: GABON: Polling booths smashed in chaotic Gabon election.
newsitem.headline: Polling booths smashed in chaotic Gabon election.

text.p: Angry voters smashed polling booths in central Gabon and held an official hostage as local elections in the oil producing country on Sunday degenerated into chaos, election officials said.
Troops backed by tanks were seen taking up positions in the sidestreets of Libreville in an apparent attempt by the authorities to prevent the chaos leading to violence.
"The election is completely chaotic. They started smashing the booths at Fougamou," National Election Committee vice-president Mengome Atome told Reuters.
Atome said a polling official had been held hostage in his office in Port Gentil, the hub of the Central African country's oil industry.
"Our officials said he had been taken hostage after voting collapsed," Atome said. There were no other details.
Witnesses told local Soleil Radio that some voting booths had been closed. Officials confirmed reports that pirate polling stations had been set up in several districts of Libreville.
Many polling stations were reopening in the late afternoon after people complained earlier that electoral officials were not prepared for voters.
Several hours after polls opened officially at 7 a.m. (0600 GMT), people headed back home as most polling stations had no ballots, voter lists or even personnel.

Oil-rich Gabon intended the municipal elections as a first test of a 1994 deal between the government and the opposition to set its democratic transition back on course and defuse sometimes bloody political rivalry.

"Many voters who have been on line at polling stations since six in the morning are heading back home," a witness said. "There is a heavy security force presence. In some stations soldiers outnumber the voters."

"The problem is not so much political as organisational," the election commission's Atome said. The commission had only 10 days to organise voting, enter all the names into the computer and hand out voter cards, he added.
The electoral commission is based in the grounds of the Republican Guard, formerly the Presidential Guard. Opposition critics say this does not bode well for the neutrality of the election results.
More than 12,000 candidates stood for election as councillors or mayors in the nine provinces of the former French colony.

There was confusion in the runup to the poll about the number of people who would be able to vote in the nation of just 1.2 million people. Voter registration ended on October 17 but election officials said computer generation of 400,000 registration and voting cards was behind schedule.
Commission documents suggested only 51,213 people had registered to vote in Libreville out of an estimated population of 300,000.
Under the 1994 Paris accords the municipal elections should have taken place in September 1995.
Legislative elections are now scheduled for November 17, a date criticised by some opposition figures who say it leaves too little time to organise.
President Omar Bongo, vice-president when Gabon gained independence in 1960, became head of state in 1968 on the death of president Leon Mba and set up a one-party state.

He began moves towards a multi-party system in 1990 after a rash of strikes and demonstrations by workers and students. Bongo won a five-year term with just over 51 percent of votes cast in 1993 elections which sparked opposition protest.
